summary.text: Convection is the movement of a fluid caused by differences in properties such as density, and it can carry heat from place to place.
In natural convection, warmer and lighter fluid rises while colder and denser fluid sinks, setting up a circulating flow.
It drives weather and ocean currents and enables fan-free cooling, but it needs gravity, so it does not occur in a free-falling space station.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: From Latin convectio, a carrying or conveying

facts.label: Where it occurs
facts.value: Atmosphere, oceans, Earth's mantle and stars

facts.label: In orbit
facts.value: None on the International Space Station

facts.label: Salty layers
facts.value: Salt water over fresher water also sets off convection

items.prompt: A thermometer in a chimney, well away from the flames, reads hotter. What carried the heat there?

options.label: Heated air that moved up the chimney
Rays from the flames reaching it directly
The metal of the grate passing it along
Smoke particles bumping into the thermometer

items.explain: Air passing near the fire became heated and carried its warmth up the chimney, which is convection.

items.prompt: On the orbiting space station, an astronaut heats a sealed pouch of water from below. Why does the hot water not rise to the top?

options.label: Water cannot expand in a sealed pouch
Without gravity, buoyancy does not drive any flow
The pouch walls block all heat transfer
Space is too cold for water to warm up

items.explain: Convection depends on gravity pulling denser fluid down, so free-fall environments have no buoyant convection.

items.prompt: Why does warm air in a room rise toward the ceiling?

options.label: It is less dense than the cooler air around it
It is attracted to the ceiling by heat
It contains more weight than cool air
It is pushed upward by the colder floor

items.explain: Warm air is less dense, so buoyancy lifts it while denser, colder air sinks, creating a circulating flow.

items.prompt: A layer of very salty water is poured gently on top of fresher water in a tank. What follows?

options.label: Nothing, because the layers stay separate forever
The fresh water sinks through the salty layer
The salty layer sinks, setting off convection
Both layers freeze at the contact line

items.explain: Salt water is heavier than fresh water, so the heavier layer on top sinks and drives convection without any temperature difference.

items.prompt: Two pots are heated the same way, one holding water and one holding thick syrup. Which develops convection less readily?

options.label: Syrup, since its stickiness resists the flow
Water, since it is lighter and holds heat in place
Both equally, since the heat input is identical
Neither, since convection only happens in gases

items.explain: Natural convection is less likely and less rapid in a more viscous (sticky) fluid.

items.prompt: A thermometer touches the metal grate of a fire but cannot see the flames. It warms. By what route did the heat arrive?

options.label: Rising currents of heated air
Radiation across the open space
Conduction through the metal
Gravity pulling heat downward

items.explain: Heat reaching a thermometer in contact with the grate has travelled through the metal, which is conduction, not convection.
